_comment: Candidate NYC <-> UN indicator pairs. Each entry declares both sides plus a human-assigned comparability grade and the reason for it. pair_probe.py verifies that both sides actually resolve and that the units agree; it does NOT assign the grade -- that stays a human judgment, recorded here and reviewable.

pairs.label: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5), annual mean

soql.$select: time_period AS yr, data_value AS value
soql.$where: name='Fine particles (PM 2.5)' AND geo_type_name='Citywide' AND measure='Annual mean'

pairs.reason: Units agree (ug/m3) and both are annual means, but the methods differ: NYC's figure comes from NYCCAS ground monitors, the UN's is a population-weighted modelled estimate. Comparable in level, not interchangeable. Chart together with the method difference stated.

pairs.label: Intentional homicide

soql.$select: date_extract_y(cmplnt_fr_dt) AS yr, count(*) AS value

pairs.reason: NYPD 'murder & non-negligent manslaughter' tracks the UNODC intentional-homicide definition closely. BLOCKER: NYC side is a count, UN side is a rate per 100,000 -- needs an annual NYC population denominator before the two can share an axis. Pre-2006 rows in this dataset carry junk incident dates (17 murders in 1990) and are excluded. Denominator: Census ACS 1-year total population. There is no ACS 1-year release for 2020, so 2020 carries no rate -- and 2020 is the year NYC homicides jumped. That gap is left empty rather than interpolated.

denominator.source: Census ACS 1-year B01003_001E, NYC place 51000 / state 36

pairs.label: Proportion of municipal waste recycled

soql.$select: substring(month,1,4) AS yr, sum(papertonscollected + mgptonscollected) / sum(refusetonscollected + papertonscollected + mgptonscollected) * 100 AS value

pairs.reason: DSNY tonnage covers DSNY-collected residential waste only -- it excludes commercial waste, which the UN municipal-waste definition includes. Derived diversion rate, not a published one; the published Recycling Diversion and Capture Rates dataset has not updated since 2020. The month field is text ('2026 / 08') so the year comes from substring, not date_extract_y. Rows before 1993 predate curbside recycling (no recycling tonnage, 1990 partial) and are excluded.

pairs.label: Road traffic deaths

soql.$select: date_extract_y(crash_date) AS yr, sum(number_of_persons_killed) AS value

denominator.source: Census ACS 1-year B01003_001E, NYC place 51000 / state 36

pairs.reason: NYC holds 11 years of rates from Vision Zero collision records; the UN holds ONE observation, 2021. That blocks a trend and not a ranking: WHO publishes a single global round, and 195 countries in that year is enough to place NYC (#18 of 196, 3.51 per 100k, beside Spain and the Netherlands, against 14.2 for the US). Originally graded BLOCKED -- the blocker was our framing, not the data. Still Tier 3: a city set against whole nations. WHO figures are modelled estimates; NYC counts collision records.

pairs.label: Child mortality (deaths)

soql.$select: year AS yr, infant_deaths AS value

pairs.reason: AGE BANDS DO NOT MATCH. The UN counts deaths under five; NYC's infant mortality dataset counts deaths under one. Both are raw counts so the units 'agree', which is exactly the trap -- a chart would look correct and compare different populations. Show side by side, never on one axis, until an under-five NYC series is sourced.

pairs.label: Maternal mortality

soql.$select: year AS yr, sum(deaths) AS value

pairs.reason: Two problems. NYC publishes pregnancy-ASSOCIATED deaths (any cause within a year of pregnancy), a deliberately broader definition than the UN's maternal mortality. And the UN rate is per 100,000 LIVE BIRTHS, not per population -- the denominator lives in a different NYC dataset (fcau-jc6k number_of_live_births). Needs a cross-dataset join before it can be charted.

pairs.label: Deaths attributable to ambient air pollution

soql.$select: time_period AS yr, data_value AS value
soql.$where: name='Deaths due to PM2.5' AND geo_type_name='Citywide'

pairs.reason: UN reports a national death COUNT attributable to ambient air pollution; NYC reports an age-adjusted RATE for ages 30+ attributable to PM2.5 specifically. Different measure, different age base, different pollutant scope. Informative side by side, not comparable on one axis.

pairs.label: Poverty
pairs.reason: NOT THE SAME CONCEPT. The UN series is the share below the INTERNATIONAL extreme-poverty line (~$2.15/day PPP), which is near zero for any US city and carries no signal. NYC's own poverty measure is a cost-of-living-adjusted threshold an order of magnitude higher. Also the NYCgov measure is published as a separate dataset per year, so there is no continuous series to query. Included as the clearest example of two numbers that share a name and measure nothing alike.

pairs.label: Inadequate housing

soql.$select: date_extract_y(inspectiondate) AS yr, count(*) AS value

pairs.reason: UN measures the SHARE OF URBAN POPULATION living in slums. NYC's nearest analogue is a COUNT of class C (immediately hazardous) housing maintenance violations -- an enforcement output, not a population share, and sensitive to inspection rates rather than to conditions alone. Directionally interesting, structurally different. Tier 2: the UN side is urban, which bundles cities with suburbs.

pairs.label: Built-up area per capita (cities)
pairs.reason: Tier 1 UN data exists with a full 2000-2025 series and city-level slices across countries, but no NYC Open Data equivalent has been identified. Candidates to investigate: PLUTO lot area aggregates, Parks Properties. Recorded so the gap is visible rather than forgotten.

pairs.label: Safely managed drinking water
pairs.reason: The UN series sits at or near 100% for the US across the whole window, as it would for NYC. A chart of two flat lines at 100 tells a policy analyst nothing. Recorded as deliberately excluded rather than overlooked -- a ceiling effect is a reason not to build a view, and that judgment should be written down.

pairs.label: Municipal waste collected

soql.$select: substring(month,1,4) AS yr, sum(coalesce(refusetonscollected,0) + coalesce(papertonscollected,0) + coalesce(mgptonscollected,0) + coalesce(resorganicstons,0) + coalesce(schoolorganictons,0) + coalesce(leavesorganictons,0) + coalesce(xmastreetons,0) + coalesce(otherorganicstons,0)) AS value

pairs.reason: The US reports this indicator to nobody -- EN_MWT_COLLV has ZERO US observations in every year, while 90 other countries report it, so NYC's only comparator is the world. Both sides are derived to kg per capita, so the raw units differ by design (UN tonnes, NYC tons). TWO CAVEATS. DSNY collects from residences and institutions only and the UN definition includes commercial waste, so NYC's figure is an UNDERCOUNT and its true rank is worse -- the opposite direction to the recycling pair, where the same gap flatters the comparator instead. And DSNY publishes 'Tons' without saying short or metric; US short tons assumed, and if they are metric every NYC figure is ~10% low.

derive.note: DSNY publishes 'Tons' without specifying short or metric; US short tons assumed. If metric, NYC figures are ~10% low.

pairs.label: Hazardous waste generated per unit of GDP
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (NYC DEP wastewater co-digestion, b3mq-yvvr) tracks monthly biogas and RNG production metrics at wastewater treatment plants -- an energy-recovery indicator, not a hazardous waste indicator. EN_HAZ_GENGDP requires Basel Convention hazardous waste generation in tonnes per million USD GDP; the biogas dataset contains no hazardous waste data of any kind.

pairs.label: Hazardous waste exported
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (DSNY disposal sites, 99xv-he3n) tracks routing of DSNY-collected municipal solid waste to domestic landfills and transfer stations. EN_HAZ_EXP measures transboundary shipments of hazardous waste under the Basel Convention. These are different regulatory regimes (Basel vs. domestic MSW) and different waste streams; DSNY does not handle Basel Convention hazardous waste.

pairs.label: Total waste generation
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (DSNY waste characterization, bibp-6ff7) consists of four snapshot composition studies (2005, 2013, 2017, 2023) giving material percentages of residential waste -- not generation volumes. Even with a volume dataset, DSNY residential collection covers roughly half of total waste generated; the UN indicator includes commercial and industrial streams invisible to DSNY.

pairs.label: Total wastewater treated
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (Watershed Water Quality -- Wastewater, icbf-663g) records chemical parameter monitoring at wastewater treatment plant effluent sites (analytes, concentrations, compliance). EN_WWT_TREAT requires volumetric flow -- cubic metres treated per year. The dataset has no flow volume columns; it answers 'how clean is the effluent,' not 'how much is treated.'

pairs.label: Hazardous waste treated or disposed, volume
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (Dewatered Solids and Biosolids Allocations, 95kh-h6zc) tracks sewage sludge management -- the solid byproduct of wastewater treatment -- in dry metric tons. Biosolids are regulated under 40 CFR Part 503 and are explicitly excluded from hazardous waste definitions under both RCRA and the Basel Convention. EN_HAZ_TRTDISV measures hazardous waste treated or disposed through approved methods; biosolids are not hazardous waste.

pairs.label: Proportion of hazardous waste treated or disposed
pairs.reason: Same dataset mismatch as EN_HAZ_TRTDISV: biosolids (95kh-h6zc) are sewage sludge, explicitly excluded from hazardous waste definitions under Basel and RCRA. Both the numerator (hazardous waste treated) and denominator (hazardous waste generated) for this proportion are absent from the biosolids dataset.

pairs.label: Hazardous waste imported
pairs.reason: Same dataset as proposed for EN_HAZ_EXP (DSNY disposal sites, 99xv-he3n). DSNY collects municipal solid waste for domestic disposal; it does not handle internationally imported hazardous waste under the Basel Convention. Transboundary hazardous waste movements occur at national level under EPA and State authority, not city level.

pairs.label: Proportion of groundwater bodies with good ambient water quality
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (Watershed Water Quality -- Limnology, 3y4p-uusw) monitors chemical and physical parameters of NYC's drinking water reservoir system -- surface water bodies. EN_H2O_GRAMBQ specifically measures groundwater bodies (aquifers). Limnology is the science of inland surface waters; groundwater is a distinct hydrological compartment with separate monitoring requirements. NYC's watershed reservoirs are not aquifers.

pairs.label: Total wastewater generated
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (NYC DEP wastewater co-digestion, b3mq-yvvr) tracks biogas production metrics -- sludge wet tons digested, RNG output, food scraps co-digested. EN_WWT_GEN requires total wastewater generated in volumetric flow units. Biogas production is a downstream energy-recovery metric at wastewater plants; it does not measure or allow estimation of influent wastewater volumes.

pairs.label: Proportion of wastewater safely treated
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (Dewatered Solids and Biosolids, 95kh-h6zc) records sludge disposal destinations in dry metric tons. EN_WWT_TREATR is a ratio of volumetric wastewater flows. Both the treated-flow numerator and the generated-flow denominator require flow data absent from the biosolids dataset.

pairs.label: Extent of human made wetlands
pairs.reason: Proposed dataset (NYC Wetlands, p48c-iqtu) classifies wetland features by vegetation and hydrological type (estuarine, emergent, forested, shrub/scrub) via remote sensing. EN_WBE_HMWTL counts hectares of human-made water bodies (reservoirs, irrigation canals, aquaculture ponds, salt pans) per SDG 6.6.1. The dataset's classification schema maps ecological type, not construction origin; no field distinguishes human-made from natural wetlands. NYC's principal human-made water bodies -- the Catskill/Delaware/Croton reservoir system -- are outside the five boroughs and outside this dataset's geographic scope.
